claims.text: The proposed coating is a nanocrystalline HEA multilayer with well-defined interfaces.
HEAs can contain BCC/HCP or BCC/FCC phase structures suitable for use as alternating layers.
The multilayer and monolithic coatings will be compared at the same overall chemistry and thickness.
Creep tests will be conducted at 750–850 °C under constant stress.
Diffusion and dislocation climb govern creep kinetics under the proposed 750–850 °C test conditions.
Chemical and crystallographic interfaces pin or deflect dislocations.
Multilayer interfaces impede dislocation climb.
Multilayer interfaces impede grain-boundary sliding.
Multilayer interfaces disrupt continuous diffusion pathways required for time-dependent deformation.
The interfaces raise the activation energy for dislocation climb and grain-boundary sliding.
Interface-induced obstruction of dislocation and diffusion processes reduces creep rate relative to a homogeneous coating.
The multilayer coating will have a delayed onset of accelerated creep relative to the monolithic coating.
The multilayer coating will have a lower steady-state creep rate than the monolithic coating.
The multilayer coating will accumulate less total creep strain than the monolithic coating.
The interface benefit is most pronounced when diffusion-controlled creep dominates.
The proposed benefit applies particularly when individual layer thicknesses are on the order of tens of nanometers.
Lower temperatures or thicker layers may reduce the creep-resistance benefit by lowering interface density or changing the controlling deformation mechanism.
Residual stresses, phase transformations, and service-induced interdiffusion may alter the proposed interface-barrier effect.
The quantitative creep reduction may vary with the HEA composition and multilayer design.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in steady-state creep rate and cumulative strain under identical conditions would falsify the proposed interface benefit.
